title: The Slow Radiators
premise: Jonah Dunmore, a translator in a fading port city, has spent thirty years converting his mother's language into English until almost nothing of it remains in his mouth. When a late-night radio program broadcasts a song he knows was written by his mother and never recorded, he discovers the singer is still alive — and that the song was left unfinished on purpose, waiting for someone to claim the missing verse. Jonah's inventory of unsaid things becomes a literal list he must work through as the city reroutes the last bus to his old neighborhood, erasing the streets where his mother sang. The novel ends with Jonah boarding that final bus, singing the lost verse aloud in a language he thought he'd surrendered, and finding that saying goodbye properly is not an ending but a way of keeping what love survives duty.
about_author: Edmund Ishikawa is the pen name of a former court interpreter who grew up between two languages in a coastal working-class family. He writes about translation not as craft but as inheritance, and lives within earshot of a bus depot.

chapters.title: The Inventory
chapters.summary: Jonah, translating a shipping contract by day, keeps a notebook of everything he never said to his mother, dead eleven years. His daughter Maren visits and asks why he never taught her the old language; he deflects with a joke. POV: Jonah. Emotional beat: the quiet shame of a man who mistakes silence for protection.

chapters.title: A Song Without a Recording
chapters.summary: Half-asleep before the radio, Jonah hears a song he knows note for note — one his mother composed in their kitchen and swore she'd never let anyone record. The announcer credits a reclusive singer, Vera Olem. Jonah checks his mother's handwriting against the lyrics printed nowhere; they match. POV: Jonah. Emotional beat: vertigo — the past asserting it was never past.

chapters.title: Vera Olem, Unlisted
chapters.summary: Jonah tracks Vera through a defunct record shop owner, Dov, who remembers both women from the old neighborhood. Vera refuses calls but leaves a message: come hear the rest of the song if you can name what's missing. POV: alternating Jonah and Dov. Emotional beat: hope arriving disguised as a dare.

chapters.title: The Rerouting Notice
chapters.summary: The transit authority announces the 14 bus line — the only route to the old neighborhood — will be permanently rerouted in three weeks. Jonah realizes the physical door to his past is closing on a schedule. He begins visiting the terminus daily, watching the route like a tide going out. POV: Jonah. Emotional beat: grief given a deadline.

chapters.title: What Mother Left Out
chapters.summary: In his mother's letters, Jonah finds the song's missing verse torn away — cut out deliberately, with scissors, decades ago. Maren helps him reconstruct context from photographs. He learns the verse was about his father, whom no one ever speaks of. POV: Jonah with Maren present. Emotional beat: the discovery that omission was an act of love, or cowardice, or both.

chapters.title: The House on Kessler Street
chapters.summary: Jonah rides the 14 to its final stop and walks to the old house, now half-demolished. A current tenant, an elderly man named Anselm, lets him inside; the kitchen tiles are still hers. Anselm hums the song without knowing its origin. POV: Jonah. Emotional beat: standing inside the architecture of memory while it is being dismantled.

chapters.title: Vera's Condition
chapters.summary: Vera finally meets Jonah and reveals she recorded the song at his mother's request — a promise that whoever came looking for it must sing the missing verse themselves, aloud, in the original language. Jonah confesses he can barely speak it anymore; words keep slipping into English mid-sentence. POV: Vera then Jonah. Emotional beat: the terrible arithmetic of what survival cost him.

chapters.title: Borrowed Words
chapters.summary: Jonah drills himself nightly with tapes, dictionaries, Maren's patient questions. Words return unevenly — he can say 'river' but not 'forgive.' Dov finds a bootleg tape of his mother singing the verse's first line. Rising tension: two days remain before the bus is rerouted and Vera leaves the city. POV: Jonah. Emotional beat: a language coming back like blood into a numb limb.

chapters.title: The Last Full Route
chapters.summary: Penultimate day. Jonah boards the 14 at dawn intending to rehearse at the terminus, but panic seizes him mid-route and he nearly gets off early — choosing, again, not to arrive. Maren, riding beside him uninvited, says the thing from his own inventory back to him. He stays on. POV: Jonah and Maren. Emotional beat: the climax of avoidance breaking.

chapters.title: Out Loud Before the Last Bus
chapters.summary: Final night of the route. At Vera's small studio above the record shop, with Maren and Dov present, Jonah sings the missing verse — imperfect, accented, whole. The song is finally complete and recorded. He rides the 14 home one last time, speaking the old language softly to Maren out the window as familiar streets slide past. POV: Jonah. Emotional beat: resolution — goodbye spoken properly becomes belonging reclaimed, not lost.
